I do not think any committee of the House could do that; a committee of the House must follow the law, and I do not think any committee can go further than a court of justice can go. The difficulty, if there is one, is in the law itself and until the law is amended anyone who finds himself in the very unfortunate position of Mr. Collins will have to submit to his fate, because that is the law.
The point I am going to bring out now is one of form, and should probably have been mentioned earlier. I respectfully submit that this petition cannot be entertained by the House because it is not supported by an affidavit, and again because no deposit is made. Mr. Collins says, "If I could secure justice under that act I would not come before parliament, but I cannot do so." Parliament answers, "We can receive the petition, but we cannot give you any more privi-10 p.m. lege than the law gives you, and under the law you are compelled first to make a deposit of $1,000 and in the 14011-293J
next place to add to your petition an affidavit." Do hon. members realize the futility of presenting a petition to this House without an affidavit? It it were not for our faith in the word of hon. members opposite who have declared that the contents of the petition are true, that petition would be thrown into the basket. It has no meaning; it is purely and simply a declaration by somebody with no proof and no evidence in support of it. The Controverted Elections Act specifically says that an election petition must be supported by an affidavit. The reason for that is very obvious; it is that a proceeding of that kind must be a serious proceeding, and must be supported by an affidavit so that it will not be a joke and, on its face, will demonstrate the prima facie truth of the allegations. This affidavit does not here exist. Then the same law says that you must deposit $1,000, in order to prove your good faith, and in order to show that you are serious. That deposit was not made in this case. So that if this petition was received, Mr. Collins, who did not go before the courts when he should have done; Mr. Collins, who had the right himself to institute proceedings-Mr. Collins, because he has not taken care of his own interests when he should have done so, would receive better treatment before this House than the man who had looked after his own interests. I have an authority here which I quoted this afternoon. It is reported in Speakers' Decisions, by L. G. Desjardins, where at page 267 I find that on March 13. 1873, the Hon. James Cock-burn, Speaker of this House, held as follows on an election petition:
In my opinion this petition being an election peti

tion, and not having .been accompanied by the required security to answer costs, is a void petition, and cannot be made the ground work of a motion.
Therefore at that time it was incumbent upon every petitioner who wanted parliament seized of an election petition to accompany his petition with a deposit of $1,000, and failing to do that, his petition was dismissed. That law has been changed, but this provision by *which the petitioner was compelled to make a deposit of $1,000 was reintroduced in the Controverted Elections Act, and therefore we have the same law on that subject to-day that we had before. What is the ground for Mr. Collins' contending that he should be put in a more favourable position before parliament than any other petitioner has been in since confederation?
I have nothing to add, Mr. Speaker. I have been strongly impressed by the arguments that Mr. Collins may be suffering an injustice; but parliament cannot place itself

in the position of a tribunal. The laws of the land have been passed to give justice to the suffering. It may be that the laws are not effective; they may be unjust, unwise, and it may be that Mr. Collins is suffering under those laws, but in my humble opinion we must follow the law. Mr. Collins could have claimed the seat for himself. He could have adopted many means of redress which he failed to adopt, and because he failed to adopt them, he now comes before parliament and wants parliament to constitute itself a court of justice. I am far from being an expert in this matter; indeed, I am sorry to say that I have not studied it very deeply, but speaking in a superficial way I must admit that I cannot see how and why parliament should come to the aid of this gentleman when there is a law .providing for his case. If that law is not sufficient, it is the law just the same for Mr. Collins as for everybody else, and he must submit to it. Mr. Collins can get something under that law even at this stage. He can get the election annulled. True, that will not give him the seat to which he thinks he is entitled, but he can get the election annulled, and that is about all he can get at this stage. Then another election will be held, and if the electors declare that Mr. Collins is their choice, he will be elected.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Labour):

subtopic: MOTION THAT PETITION OF J. A. COLLINS BE READ AND RECEIVED
speechtext:
There are certain points to which I would like to refer before the debate closes. I feel that I should say a word in regard to this matter, partly because I think everything that can be said in defence of a member of this House who is not in a position to stand up in his place and defend himself should be stated by other hon. members. No man on either side of this House will contend for one moment that the gentleman who has been returned by the regular electoral officers for Peace River in the last election has not been returned in the same manner and by similar
machinery to that by which all the other members of the House are returned. We start out with that as a basis of our discussion. The officers appointed by the crown have found him to be entitled to the seat for that constituency, and I must say that the onus is very strongly against anyone who asserts the contrary.
What is the object of the present petition? Hon. members will bear in mind that on the 6th of May the Speaker of this House, after a very exhaustive argument, declared that the petition which was then offered to the House should not be received. The reasons why it should not be received were put very clearly by Mr. Speaker at that time. Those reasons were perfectly correct, and I submit must have carried conviction to hon. members on aU sides of the House. The reasons were that years ago this House in its wisdom decided that controverted elections, and the trial of the question as to the right of a member to hold a seat in this House, should be heard1 by some tribunal other than that made up of his fellow members in this House. Surely nobody here is going to argue that we should go back to the old law, in existence before the Controverted Elections Act was .passed, which placed the trial of any member against whom a petition might be lodged in the hand's of his friends and his opponents in this House. Nobody will argue seriously that we want to go back and make this a tribunal for trying whether or not my friend or my political opponent shall sit in this chamber or remain out of it. That is the reason why all the authorities make it abundantly clear that a petition which attacks the right of a member to hold his seat shall not be received. We can either try in this House the right of our fellows to hold a seat or we cannot. If we cannot try them, why make an abortive attempt to do so? Why receive a petition that is going to cast a reflection upon the right of any member to hold a seat in this House if we have not the right to proceed and1 try it out? Will any of my hon. friends argue that they desire to go back to the old system of having this House turned into an election court? Because that is what it amounts to. We got away from that years ago, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, with great respect, that this House is not going to take any steps which would mean a return to that old procedure. That is the reason why a petition which has for its object the trial of the right of any member to hold his seat in the House-^apart from disqualification such as has been referred to, penal offence or anything of that kind-can-
Peace River Election

not foe received here. When the petition is tendered' and examined by the Clerk of Petitions, the examination is for the purpose of seeing whether or not it is a petition proper to be received. If we cannot deal with it then it should not be received.
Let us consider what the object of this petition is, I ask my hon. friends who argue that it should not be received: What does this petition ask for? It is true it complains about the conduct of the electoral officers, but what is the kernel of the whole-petition? It states:
Your petitioner prays that the House of 'Commons will investigate the conduct of the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada, the returning officer for the electoral district of Peace River, Edward Henry Sheppard, aforesaid, the deputy returning officer, Peter A. Robb, aforesaid, and such other officer or officers as may be necessary in connection with the establishment of a polling place at Brule Mines poll No. 4 aforesaid and the taking of, .the counting and recounting the votes east at such poll in the electoral district of Peace River aforesaid, and that such Chief Eleotoral Officer, returning officer, deputy returning officer or other officer or officers be directed to take such action as may ibe requisite and necessary to secure the return to the House of Commons of the candidate who secured the greatest number of votes cast by the electors of the electoral district of Peace River on the 29th of October, 1925, aforesaid.
That means that the petitioner asks this House to try out the question of which candidate received the greatest number of votes and who is entitled to a seat in this House. It means that if the House finds that Collins received more votes than Kennedy, the officer should be instructed to make a declaration declaring Collins and not Kennedy entitled to the seat. That is exactly what this House decided on the 6th May it could not do, and that was the reason why the petition which was then presented could not be received.
When you come to size up the arguments of hon. gentlemen who argue that this petition should be received, they say that it should be received because it- asks for an inquiry into the conduct of officials who conducted, the election. It is true it asks for that; but in addition and as the main part of the petition it asks that it should be found that the candidate who received the greatest number of votes should be declared elected. That means possibly that somebody who now has the seat should be put out and somebody else put in. What was the objection before to receiving the petition? It was that it violated the rules and therefore was not properly receivable. Do my ihon. friends who argued on behalf of the petition which was declared bad on the sixth May, say that by tacking on to a bad petition some clauses which are good they are going to make the part of the 
petition which was bad on the 6th May, good now? That is what this means. It is on account of the bad parts in the petition, the parts that are not receivable, that it could not be received before. Unless the whole petition can be received, it cannot be received at all. You cannot receive part of it; if there is in that petition anything that is objectionable and cannot be received, the whole petition must be rejected.
I took care to look at the date of this petition and I find that on the outside of it is dated the 28th May, 1926, twenty-two days after the previous decision. Nobody can read this petition without realizing what the petitioner had in mind. It is quite clear, when 3'ou take the date into consideration, that the petition seeks just what I have already said

by tacking on to the objecionable part something that is unobjectionable, to get in the whole petition. That cannot be done.
A great deal has been said about the fact that in the election court you cannot try out the question of how anybody voted. The section of the act referred to is section 221, which says that no person shall be asked how he voted. What was the object of that? It was made perfectly clear by a very learned judge in the Haldimand case. I quote it in his words, which are much better than any I could see:
As to .the petitioner's claim for the seat, it must be dismissed.
The evidence of thirty-six voters to show how they had voted for Colter at polling division, No. 2, Oneida, was properly held not admissible by the learned judge at the trial.
Had the learned judge permitted the inquiry to have been prosecuted as the petitioner desired, it would have in effect disclosed not merely how those willing to tell had voted, but practically how every man at the poll had voted, because if out of one hundred votes fifty are found to have voted for A and fifty for B and the fifty who voted for A are called and expressing their willingness to tell do tell that they voted for him, it at once becomes known who the fifty were who voted for B.
Let us take another example where the majority in the election is small. I know my hon. friends are pursuing this very seriously with a view possibly to remedying a defect which they suggest now exists in the law. I ask them to consider this: Does any defect exist in the law as it now stands? Does any hon. member suggest that it would be in the interest of justice or of candidates who occasionally have to fight election contests to have the law changed1? Supposing a man is elected by a majority of five, and supposing that at a certain poll he is credited with twenty votes and thirty people come in and say: I voted for that candidate. If that were

to be allowed, in many cases where there are not many votes in a poll it wiould be possible to get enough electors whose names are on the lists to come in and pledge their oaths that they voted for this man and he lost his seat. That is not what the legislators intended. That is the very evil which the people who framed this aict intended to avoid. The right of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) or of any other hon. member to hold his seat should! not depend upon whether or not ten, fifteen or twenty people are willing to come in and swear that in a certain polling division they cast their votes in one way and the record would show that they had not been counted. That is the object of the law and' it is made very clear in the decision of Mr. Justice Taschereau in the Haldimand case, volume 15, of the Supreme Court reports.

speechtext: I am about to ask the question. Does he object to these little interruptions for fear they may hurt his argument and spoil the effect of his speech?

subtopic: MOTION THAT PETITION OF J. A. COLLINS BE READ AND RECEIVED
speechtext: I offered the hon. gentleman another chance to come within eight years of this case, but he has failed miserably. No, interruptions never hurt an argument-

subtopic: MOTION THAT PETITION OF J. A. COLLINS BE READ AND RECEIVED
speechtext: The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) wandered two hundred years away from it.

subtopic: MOTION THAT PETITION OF J. A. COLLINS BE READ AND RECEIVED
speechtext:
-if those interruptions are pertinent. But if the present interruptions are intended to divert the argument from its purpose they will fail. If the hon. gentleman cannot interrupt with something that bears upon the subject the best thing he can do is to keep his seat.
Now, under the petition of Page, or under any petition that Collins might have entered, there could be no remedy in the world of any character whatever, for the wrong which has been done. Collins could not do anything to have the seat vacated, but if he could it would not be justice. It would not be justice to Collins. There is therefore no remedy before the courts; there is no remedy whatever outside this parliament. The only means by which this wrong can be redressed, this outrage as heinous as any ever per-

Peace River Election

petrated in the political history of this country, must be taken by parliament. The only place where the cause can be heard and the remedy applied is in this House. No hon. gentleman who has spoken opposite has dared to suggest that there is any effective remedy, indeed, any remedy at all anywhere else in our Dominion; and knowing there is no other remedy parliament purposes to inform Collins that he must rest under this vicious wrong. Is this gross outrage, this black brazen fraud which has been perpetrated in order to enable a government to sit .in office, not to be redressed? It is for the House now to decide.
